quote: Compaction can, however, silently remove task constraints: on ProgramBench, the first compaction summary already drops about one third of the task's anticheating rules on average, and this rises monotonically with the number of compactions. On real user-agent sessions from SWE-chat, instructions about how the agent should work and what it should not do are dropped around 6 times more than specifications of what to build.
observation: Compaction's measurable damage lands on prohibitions and process rules, which no benchmark checks, while objectives and on-disk progress survive; the same paper finds no method beats default self-summarization on frontier models at a fixed scaffold (OpenCode, 5 strategies, 3 models), so the dense recipe literature evaluated on small models and synthetic traces has no shown gain where it matters.
who_strains: Compaction-recipe authors (94 hits in W41's window); scaffold builders (OpenCode, Claude Code, Codex); benchmark owners (PaperBench, ProgramBench, PostTrainBench)
question: Do agentic benchmarks measure compaction loss at all? Constraint retention as the missing axis of long-horizon evaluation.
density_hint: Salle, Bhatnagar, Bethge, Abdelnabi, Andriushchenko (Tubingen/ELLIS); Compact-Bench 2610.31710; 2610.08722 (590 AppWorld boundaries, W41); Compaction Laundering 2610.29869 (forged user turns survive flattening harnesses 87-100%)
mechanism_version: Which content class a self-summary drops is set by what the summary prompt asks to keep (objective, progress); prohibitions have no slot in the summary schema and no trace on disk, so the loss is a schema property of the scaffold, not a property of model size.
free_data_check: SWE-chat sessions are public; ProgramBench's anticheating rules are public text; the paper's OpenCode runs (3 models x 5 strategies x 3 benchmarks) if released. No training needed.
method_consequence: If constraint loss is schema-driven, a compaction prompt with a pinned constraint ledger fixes it without training and benchmarks add a constraint-retention score; if it tracks the model, compaction becomes a training target (L4 lab-contested).

quote: LLM summaries retain at most 16.0% of recurring details, compared with 79.1% for mechanical extraction; production summaries retain 15.7% at the first boundary. Failures recur across methods: one repair is damaged by 13/14 backbones, and another by all 5 prompts. These results show that reliable compaction requires preserving the progress needed to complete a task, and that retaining relevant information alone does not ensure successful continuation.
observation: Detail retention and task continuation come apart: mechanical extraction keeps five times the details and still does not decide continuation, and particular repairs die under almost every summarizer, so compaction damage is a task property before it is a summarizer property.
who_strains: Scaffold builders (Kimi Code, Claude Code prompts compared); summarizer-backbone vendors (14 compared); compaction-recipe authors
question: What in a compaction summary predicts continuation success? Task-level, not summarizer-level, compaction damage.
density_hint: Sun, Cai, Zhao, Zhou, Li (USTC); 2610.31778; 2610.08722; dataset caijanfeng/compact-bench (35 repairs, 146 sessions, 106 production chains)
mechanism_version: A continuation fails when the summary omits the one state variable the next action depends on (a partial edit, a failing test name); which repairs are fragile is set by how much of their state lives only in the conversation rather than on disk.
free_data_check: Compact-Bench is released with paired full-history and summary-only continuations; a fragility predictor (in-context vs on-disk state share) can be fitted on it with no new runs.
method_consequence: A fragility predictor decides when to compact and what to pin; none if damage is random across tasks.

quote: across 720 runs, the single largest prompt used only 5.75% of it. Yet a third of all tool results (3,827 of 11,189) were cut before they reached the model, and every cut result became broken JSON. [...] the cut's real cost appears first as extra work, not as wrong answers: 43% more tool calls, twice the computation, and yield falling from 0.61 to 0.31. [...] Whether the data cut truly causes the accuracy drop is still an open question.
observation: Harnesses slice tool output at a fixed character length even when the context window is empty, and the loss shows up as extra tool calls and compute before it shows up as wrong answers, so cost-per-task carries a harness-truncation term that no benchmark attributes.
who_strains: Harness builders (seven frameworks surveyed, two cut the same unsafe way); cost leaderboards; the authors (question left open)
question: How much agentic compute is re-fetching what the harness threw away? Tool-output truncation as an unattributed cost term.
density_hint: Sehgal, Panahandeh, Ezzati-Jivan; 2610.04433 (harness tokens, W41 #2); 2610.32483 (model-harness fit)
mechanism_version: Fixed-length slicing deletes whatever sits at the end of a serialized result, so the loss is positional and correlated with when the evidence was generated, not with relevance; the agent compensates by re-querying, which is where the cost goes.
free_data_check: The paper's 864 replayed results; public SWE-agent / OpenHands trajectories carry observation-truncation markers in the log (SWE-bench experiments repository), so truncation frequency and the following re-query rate can be counted without runs.
method_consequence: If truncation causes the yield drop, tail-aware or structured truncation is a free fix and cost tables need a truncation column; if not, none.

quote: With mini-SWE-agent on 100 SWE-bench Verified instances, keeping only the last five observations (Mask-5) cuts Eager's prompt volume by 33.3% but loses 135.9k reusable tokens per task. Uncached prefill rises by 608.5%, the energy proxy by 125.6%, and the policy misses the quality gate. Policies thus save physical work by shortening the trajectory and can multiply it by editing reusable history.
observation: Token-count accounting and executed-prefill accounting rank context policies in opposite directions, so every 'saves N% tokens' claim for a context policy is unproven about cost until re-scored under a caching runtime.
who_strains: Context-policy authors; cost leaderboards that count full tokens (HAL); serving teams
question: Do token-saving context policies increase physical compute? Re-scoring context management under prefix caching.
density_hint: Yu, Ma, Yu, Yuan, Lin, Zhang, Zhao (UCSD); TurnCost 2610.15093; 2610.04433; Cache Engineering 2610.28577; vLLM AgentX
mechanism_version: Any edit to the prompt prefix invalidates the KV cache from the edit point onward, so a policy that rewrites history converts cached reads into uncached prefill; the sign of the cost change is decided by where in the prefix the edit lands, not by how many tokens it removes.
free_data_check: Public trajectories with per-step prompts (HAL rollouts, SWE-rebench, TurnCost's 600 trajectories) can be re-scored under a cache model with no new runs.
method_consequence: Context-policy papers report executed prefill, not tokens; trainers choose compaction points that preserve the cached prefix (append-only summaries).

quote: Median observations contain only 118-286 tokens [...] 98.6% of input tokens are served from a prefix cache, so flat input pricing overestimates loop cost by roughly 7x on average under near-ideal caching. [...] turn count explains 84% of the variance in log trajectory cost, compared with 4% for mean observation size [...] though we do not establish that turns can be removed while holding task success fixed.
observation: On 600 public coding-agent trajectories cost is a turn-count phenomenon and the cached share is near total, which answers W41 #2's prefix-re-read question (98.6%) on this corpus and leaves the live one, whether turns are removable at fixed success, explicitly open.
who_strains: HAL and SWE-rebench cost columns (full-price accounting); observation-compression and turn-routing authors
question: How many agent turns are removable at fixed success? Turn redundancy as the dominant and unmeasured cost lever.
density_hint: Kumar, Pandey (TurnCost tool released); 2610.04433; 2610.34763; 2609.23790 Total Cost of Agency
mechanism_version: Per-turn cost is the uncached suffix plus a fixed per-call overhead, so cost scales with turns; turns are set by the agent's loop-exit and re-checking habits, not by observation size.
free_data_check: The 600 released trajectories plus the TurnCost re-scorer; HAL rollouts; the turn-redundancy count (repeated reads, repeated test runs) is a replay-free annotation.
method_consequence: If a large share of turns are redundant, a turn penalty in RL or a loop-exit rule is the recipe change; if not, cost work moves to the uncached suffix and there is none.

quote: modifying the trajectory prefix invalidates subsequent cached states and triggers costly re-prefilling of retained context. [...] we [...] identify history dependence as a serving challenge: identical token sequences can yield different cache states under different cache operation sequences, making prefix matching insufficient for correct cache reuse.
observation: Serving stacks assume a prompt's token prefix identifies its KV state; once agents edit their own cache that assumption fails, and a tool-response rolling-drop policy cuts cost 27.7% over threshold-triggered summarization, so text-level compaction may be the wrong layer for cost.
who_strains: Serving teams (vLLM, SGLang prefix caching); scaffold builders doing text compaction
question: What share of agentic serving cost is re-prefill triggered by context edits, and does cache-level control beat text-level compaction at equal quality?
density_hint: Fu et al. (Tsinghua NICS, thu-nics/AKV); 2610.34763; vLLM AgentX (Marconi-style retention); W41 KV-reuse group (ReCache, Leyline, StepKV, CommitKV)
mechanism_version: Text-level compaction is a prefix edit and therefore a cache flush; cache-level drop and reposition keep the trajectory text, so the prefix match survives and the only cost is the attention mask.
free_data_check: None without serving logs; AKV code is public, so a replay of public trajectories through it measures re-prefill share.
method_consequence: If cache operations win at equal quality, training-time compaction should emit cache operations rather than summaries; if not, none.

quote: Median of 43 turns per session [...] median input of 142K tokens and median output of 444 tokens [...] Prefix-cache hit rate above 96% [...] 44% of sessions contain at least one subagent [...] all of these policies underperformed simple session-aware sticky routing [...] The comparison is about serving cost, not model quality.
observation: The serving community now has a trace-level description of agentic load (SemiAnalysis AgentX) and reports 14.6x-106x serving-cost advantages for open models against an API price while stating the comparison excludes quality; cost per solved task is still unreported anywhere. Missed by the W41 harvest.
who_strains: vLLM, SemiAnalysis, open-model vendors (DeepSeek, MiniMax, Moonshot); buyers comparing API and self-hosting
question: Cost per solved task, not tokens per GPU-second: does the serving-cost ordering of open models survive task success?
density_hint: vLLM/SemiAnalysis AgentX; Together coding-agent benchmark (2026-05-19: prompts 45k-200k tokens, $0.029 vs $0.097 per request, no cache-hit rate); HAL cost frontier
mechanism_version: Tokens per GPU-second is maximized by high concurrency and a 512-token long-prefill cap that raises TTFT for the long request; agent task success depends on latency only through timeouts, so the two orderings diverge exactly where timeouts decide outcomes.
free_data_check: AgentX traces are public; HAL per-task cost and success; a quality-gated re-ranking needs one benchmark run per serving configuration.
method_consequence: A quality-gated serving benchmark; none for training recipes.

quote: the high-performance baseline's train-inference KL rose from 2e-3 to 29.9 while reward fell back [...] the consistent run's SWE-bench Pro score holds while the baseline's drops from 0.56 to 0.22 [...] TIS or MIS reduce the effect of the mismatch but do not remove it [...] neither baseline was thoroughly tuned or explored: each ran a single configuration
observation: A serving team shows an agentic SWE RL run (Nemotron, 32 tasks x 8 trajectories per step, remote sandboxes) collapsing from numerics mismatch alone and a bitwise-consistent run holding at 87.5-91.3% of rollout throughput, with both baselines untuned, so how much published agentic-RL instability is numerics is now a live, unmeasured number.
who_strains: vLLM, NVIDIA (Nemotron), verl and Megatron maintainers; every open agentic-RL report that uses importance-sampling corrections
question: How much of agentic RL instability is train-inference mismatch? An audit of open recipes under bitwise-consistent rollouts.
density_hint: vLLM PR 61551 and the C0-C10 consistency skill; Thinking Machines batch invariance (2025-09-10, W41 L78); TIS/MIS; FlashREINFORCE; InterQ-RL 2610.35303 (quantized rollouts as a second mismatch channel compounding over turns)
mechanism_version: With MoE routing a small logit difference flips the expert combination (about 7% of tokens per update at 4 updates per step), so the sampled token's training probability comes from a different sub-network: off-policy by construction, compounded over long agent trajectories.
free_data_check: The released recipes and both run logs; any verl run can be rerun with the consistency flag, so the audit is one flag per published recipe.
method_consequence: If mismatch explains most instability, importance-correction papers are measuring their own fix for a systems bug and recipes must report train-inference KL; if not, none.
positioning: lab-contested on the fix; lab-adjacent on the audit

quote: mild policy staleness offers only limited training efficiency gains, whereas aggressive asynchrony can degrade model quality and yields diminishing efficiency gains. [...] unlike existing RL frameworks which consume each trajectory only once, experience replay of recent trajectories enables effective sample reuse, thereby amortizing the high cost of rollout generation without incurring excessive policy staleness.
observation: A systems paper states that staleness has a narrow useful band, against Prime Intellect's 'four steps behind' and PACE's accuracy gains, and replaces it with replay, a second off-policy source whose staleness per trajectory length is not reported; W41 #9's length-censoring question now has a replay variant.
who_strains: Async RL systems (ReFlow, StaleFlow, PACE, verl full-async, Prime Intellect); multi-turn agentic RL users
question: What is the staleness-quality frontier on agentic tasks, and does replay reuse trade one length censoring for another?
density_hint: Tian, Su, Xu, Diao, Qian, Zhao, Zhou, Zhou; PACE 2609.36830; StaleFlow 2601.12784; INTELLECT-3 2512.16144; verl v0.7 (full async, partial rollouts, staleness control as roadmap)
mechanism_version: Replayed trajectories carry importance ratios that shrink with age and with length, so the effective sample is again short-biased; the throughput gain is bought with a weight distribution nobody logs.
free_data_check: None public; the per-trajectory log (length, age at consumption, ratio) is free on any instrumented run (W41 #9 protocol).
method_consequence: W41 #9's measurement extends to replay weights; if length-neutral, the staleness debate stays an accuracy question.

quote: the recipe and infrastructure needed for a strong reinforcement-learning baseline remain difficult to reproduce. This makes gains from new algorithms or data hard to distinguish from improvements to an under-tuned baseline. [...] No single component is new, yet together they form the missing foundation. [...] stronger tests reduce apparent training-task mastery.
observation: An industry team (Snowflake) reaches 62.0% on SWE-bench Verified at 4B with no new algorithm, matching a concurrent method (FrogNano 61.5%) at one-sixth the rollouts, which says a large share of published agentic-RL algorithm gains is baseline tuning and that test strength changes what 'mastery' reads as.
who_strains: Agentic-RL method papers and their reviewers; open labs (SkyRL, DeepSWE, verl recipes)
question: How much of reported agentic-RL algorithm gain survives a tuned asynchronous baseline? A definitive re-run.
density_hint: Liu, Wang, Lian, Shu, Li, Yan, Zhang, He (Snowflake); FrogNano; SkyRL; DeepSWE; R2E-Gym; SWE-rebench V2; Scale-SWE
mechanism_version: Gated reward, importance-weight control and engine alignment each remove a failure that early reward curves hide; an under-tuned baseline leaves them in, and any method that incidentally fixes one of them claims the gain as its own.
free_data_check: Arctic-SWE recipe and checkpoints; R2E-Gym; one re-run per method paper on the tuned baseline (about 300 GPU-hours each at 4B).
method_consequence: Method papers report against the tuned baseline; the L2 definitive-comparison shape now has a public anchor.

quote: 111 evaluation settings yield 52,168 trajectories. Harness rankings vary across models and benchmarks; task performance and valid completion can favor different pairings, and similar task scores can accompany distinct execution profiles.
observation: Valid completion (the agent finishing and delivering anything evaluable) is a separate axis from task score and reorders harness-model pairs, so leaderboards fold crash-type failures into wrong-answer failures and the W41 'infrastructure failures counted as policy failures' item is now a measured harness property.
who_strains: Harness builders (OpenCode, Codex CLI, Pi CLI, DeepAgents); leaderboards; W41 #3
question: What fraction of agentic benchmark failures are invalid completions, and do leaderboards reorder when they are separated from wrong answers?
density_hint: Zhang et al.; 2610.00917 harness reversal (W41 #3); 2610.00651 variance decomposition; 2610.04433
mechanism_version: Harness-specific loop exits (turn caps, tool errors, context overflow) end runs before submission; these move with the model-harness pairing, not with the model, so the score difference is partly an exit-policy difference.
free_data_check: The 52,168 trajectories if released; HAL rollouts record exit reasons; Terminal-Bench team-verified runs carry timeouts.
method_consequence: Report valid-completion rate beside score; in training, treat invalid completions as no-signal rather than failure.

quote: naive success rates alone do not fully characterize whether optimized harness yields more reliable success on tasks already within reach (elicitation) or a broader range of solvable tasks (expansion). [...] we find that pass@1 advantages of harness over stronger interventions can reverse at larger attempt budgets and aggregate gains conceal shortfalls on hard tasks
observation: The sharpening-versus-expansion question of RL is now asked of harness optimization and the answer has the same shape, pass@1 gains that reverse at larger k, so harness-search and self-improving-agent papers report sharpening as capability.
who_strains: Harness-optimization and self-evolving agent authors; W41 #7
question: Does harness optimization expand the reachable task set or only sharpen pass@1? pass@k accounting for scaffolds.
density_hint: Kim, Seo, Kim, Oh, Lee, Kim, Koo, Kim; Sharpening Tax 2610.01509; 2610.04158; harness-policy optimization 2610.22791
mechanism_version: An optimized harness adds fixed procedures that raise success on tasks the base model sometimes solves and cannot create solutions it never samples; at large k the plain model recovers the gap.
free_data_check: No public pass@k for harness-search results; reruns at k=16-64 on existing harness benchmarks.
method_consequence: Self-improvement loops that select on pass@1 select for sharpening; select on pass@k or on hard-task coverage.

quote: Independent review by a critic offers a more favorable accuracy-cost tradeoff, improving average accuracy by 5.9-9.5 percentage points on TB and 3.9-6.6 on SWE at 1.13-1.25 and 1.00-1.04 times baseline cost, respectively. [...] Completion gates can yield larger gains but may substantially increase cost.
observation: A 17-design study on seven frontier models finds independent review the best accuracy-per-cost verification layer, at inference and with the critic drawn from the same model family, which sharpens W41 #5: independence of context is now measured, independence of weights at training time still is not.
who_strains: Harness builders; Alibaba (authors); PPO-style critic lines (W41 #5)
question: Is the review gain from independent context or independent weights? Separating the two in critic-gated agent loops.
density_hint: Zhang, Zhu, Lin, Cardie, Ding, Zhou (Alibaba/Cornell); Probe-and-Resume 2610.21088; Leni 2607.17044; Devin Review (W41 L87)
mechanism_version: A fresh-context critic cannot inherit the generator's unverified beliefs, so it catches errors the generator rationalized; shared weights share priors, so the catch rate has a ceiling set by shared blind spots that a different-family critic would not have.
free_data_check: The paper's Terminal-Bench and SWE-bench Verified runs if released; otherwise one benchmark, four critic arms (same/other family x fresh/shared context).
method_consequence: If context suffices, critic independence at training time is cheap (fresh context, same weights); if weights matter, policy-initialised PPO critics are structurally weak and W41 #5's arm (b) is the recipe.

quote: the agent's observations omit environment state needed for evaluation, and intermediate states offer limited evidence of whether a trajectory will succeed. At intermediate states, critics rank continuations only modestly better than chance, and environment access improves this little.
observation: In terminal environments mid-trajectory value estimation is near chance even with environment access, so the assumption behind learned critics and process rewards, that partial progress is readable, is contradicted at inference time on Terminal-Bench 2.1.
who_strains: Critic and process-reward method authors (L2); test-time search papers (MCTS over agents)
question: Is mid-trajectory value predictable at all in partially observed computer-use tasks? A ceiling for critics before any training.
density_hint: Xu, Ge, Guan, Li, Timmaraju, Wu, Kaffes (Columbia); FOCUS 2610.35801 (builds a critic on compaction-induced segment boundaries, +7.2 on BrowseComp-Plus at 9B); W41 #5
mechanism_version: The state that decides success (hidden files, process state) is not in the observation stream and the trajectory text is uninformative about it until a terminal claim, so a critic reading text predicts from a censored view; probing a forked state is the only channel that adds information.
free_data_check: Terminal-Bench 2.1 public runs with per-step logs; the paper's MCTS node scores if released; a critic-vs-chance curve by step index needs no training.
method_consequence: If near chance holds, credit over steps is bounded and critics belong only at claimed-done states; if a probing critic recovers signal, environment access is the recipe.

quote: Across five frontier agents, success drops by 20.6--53.5 percentage points on DeepSWE and 20.6--34.9 points on Terminal-Bench relative to a Clean Start, and agent rankings on DeepSWE reverse. [...] On DeepSWE, in 58.9--88.2% of failed runs, they submit with exactly the same tests failing, although they pass most of these tests from a Clean Start.
observation: Every SWE benchmark starts clean, and the moment an agent inherits a predecessor's failed work it accepts it as the task definition; this acceptance bias is the same move as trusting a compaction summary or a subagent's return, and no benchmark scores it.
who_strains: Benchmark owners (SWE-bench, Terminal-Bench); multi-session and multi-agent product teams; W41 #4
question: Does acceptance bias transfer across handoffs? Inherited state as the untested starting condition of long-horizon agents.
density_hint: Li et al.; SWE-Shift 2610.32196 (mid-execution changes: GPT-6 Astra 67.35% to 24.79%, zero paired success on tool/session changes); 2607.25152 stagnation (W41)
mechanism_version: The agent reads the workspace diff as evidence of what was done and does not re-derive the request's test set, so inherited failing tests are read as pre-existing and self-verification anchors on the predecessor's claim.
free_data_check: 198 Residual States released; five agents' trajectories if released; the same protocol runs on compaction summaries (Compact-Bench) with no new states.
method_consequence: If residual starts in the RL pool remove the bias, it is a data fix and W41 #4's overclaiming is the same mechanism; if not, handoff protocols need an explicit re-derivation step.

quote: 15.2% of all runs incur CD, with risk concentrated in ambiguity tasks (38.8% violation rate) while non-ambiguous traps average 8.4% CD. Among goal-satisfied runs, 12.8% still produce unauthorized writes. [...] CD rates vary by 4.7x across models at comparable goal rates
observation: Outcome-graded tool-use benchmarks count a run as success when it also wrote to the wrong object or over-scoped; collateral damage varies 4.7x across models at equal goal rates, so the goal reward of tau-style environments is blind to a model-level trait.
who_strains: Tool-use benchmark owners (tau-family, AgentDojo); RL teams training on goal rewards
question: Does outcome-reward RL raise collateral damage? Side-effect rate across base to RL checkpoints at fixed goal rate.
density_hint: Huang, Chen, Liang, Ma, Yang, Ke, Tan, Sun; AgentDojo; 2610.22243 shortcut sensitivity in agent-safety evals; tau2-bench
mechanism_version: A goal reward is indifferent to extra writes, so an action policy that over-acts under ambiguity is never penalized, and RL sharpens whatever base habit exists.
free_data_check: SABench traces and oracle released (2,211 model-task pairs); public base-to-RL agent pairs can be run on it at inference cost only.
method_consequence: A side-effect term in the reward if the RL arm rises; none if collateral damage is a base-model trait.

quote: intrinsic and extrinsic evaluation diverge by an average of 16 percentage points, with 44% of trajectories exceeding meaningful divergence thresholds. Diagnostic decomposition reveals that the system correctly classifies memory operations (create, update, reinforce, supersede) only 20% of the time, a failure entirely invisible to extrinsic evaluation
observation: Agent-memory systems are graded by downstream question answering, and that grade hides a 20% correct rate on the memory operations themselves, so the memory benchmarks the field ranks on measure retrieval and generation, not memory.
who_strains: Memory-system vendors (Mem0, Zep); memory benchmarks (LoCoMo); L4 recipe authors
question: Does downstream QA measure agent memory at all? Intrinsic memory-store audits against extrinsic scores.
density_hint: Toma, de Kernier, Ply, Matei; MemoryTax 2610.29823; MCCL 2610.29357 ('Whether memory can drive genuine continual learning remains an open question'); W41 L4 density
mechanism_version: A strong reader reconstructs answers from raw documents retrieved by chance, masking a broken store; the break is visible only when a fact evolves and the stale version is still retrievable.
free_data_check: FEB-30 and its generator are released; any memory system can be audited at inference cost.
method_consequence: Memory training objectives on operation correctness rather than QA; none if intrinsic and extrinsic re-converge on harder QA.

quote: Agent memory is a costly patch for a weak model: Mem0 beats full context only with GPT-4o-mini, and its build alone costs more than a whole full-context rollout. Agent memory also has a ceiling, set by the model that writes it: a stronger reader does not recover what a weaker writer left out.
observation: On one conversation and one run per cell, designed memory loses to a coding agent searching raw history on both accuracy and cost once the model is frontier-class; the bitter-lesson claim with the thinnest evidence base in this set, and nobody has run it at scale.
who_strains: Memory-system vendors; L4 recipe authors; coding-agent builders (Pi, Codex, Claude Code)
question: Is designed agent memory a weak-model patch? A cost-accuracy frontier of memory systems against raw-history search across model generations.
density_hint: Peng (single author, LoCoMo, 419 turns, 152 questions); 2610.22209; Stratum 2610.36153 (repository memory); W41 L4
mechanism_version: The writer's extraction is lossy at write time and irreversible; search over raw history is lossless and its cost falls with caching, so the crossover moves with model strength and cache price.
free_data_check: LoCoMo is public; the study needs the full conversation set and seeds (the paper has one conversation, one run) at inference cost only.
method_consequence: If confirmed, self-written memory (L4) is trained as a search policy over raw history; if not, none.

quote: Reducing these limits too much may prevent the constraint solver from converging and can lead to inaccurate or unstable simulation. [...] once all worlds have converged the solver can early exit [...] In practice, selecting good values typically involves trial-and-error. [...] If warnings are disabled and Data.overflow is not checked, overflows will lead to undefined behavior.
observation: The engine's own documentation names three silent fidelity knobs (iteration caps that stop convergence; fixed contact and constraint buffers whose overflow is undefined behaviour unless polled, and polling costs a device sync the RL guidance says to avoid every step; a solver that exits only when all worlds converge, i.e. waits for the slowest world) and gives no measurement of what any of them does to a trained policy. Missed by the W41 harvest.
who_strains: MJWarp and Newton maintainers (DeepMind, NVIDIA); every Isaac Lab, MJX and MuJoCo Playground user
question: What do RL policies learn from dropped contacts? Buffer-overflow and iteration-cap artifacts in GPU-batched MuJoCo, measured on the states policies visit.
density_hint: GPUSimBench 2607.13059; GPUPhysBench 2609.35639; IndustReal/SAPU 2305.17110; themes.yaml L5 instruments (per-step audit, exploit share rho)
mechanism_version: An overflowed world keeps stepping with missing constraints, so penetration becomes free and return rises on exactly those steps; an iteration-capped world returns an unconverged impulse that softens contact; both are rewarded and both are invisible unless Data.overflow and solver residuals are logged per step.
free_data_check: None public; the instrumentation is free on any run (Data.overflow bitmask per world; contact and constraint counts via mjwarp-testspeed --measure_alloc; the all-worlds early exit is the straggler measurement L5 needs).
method_consequence: Per-step overflow and residual logging as a training-time audit, with the per-world iteration distribution as the scheduler's input; if exploit share is zero, L5's audit has no consumer on MJWarp.
positioning: off-radar for LLM labs; lab-adjacent to engine builders

quote: A large value will slow down the simulation, while a too small value may lead to missing constraints. [...] Keeping this number low is important for performance. [...] Enabling ls_parallel provides a performance boost, but at the cost of some simulation stability. [...] Tuning these parameters can have a significant impact on both simulation performance and behaviour.
observation: The RL framework's transition guide tells users to keep line-search iterations low and to trade stability for a parallel line search, with no number for the behaviour change, no defaults stated, and the fuller guide 'planned for an upcoming release'.
who_strains: Isaac Lab users (every Newton-backed RL run); NVIDIA
question: Throughput versus verified fidelity per solver setting: the frontier Isaac Lab's defaults sit on.
density_hint: Erez, Tassa, Todorov ICRA 2015 (CPU-era frontier); GPUSimBench; L5 frontier instrument
mechanism_version: A parallel line search evaluates candidate steps simultaneously and accepts without the sequential guarantee, so the solver can accept a worse step; fewer line-search iterations leave the Newton step unconverged on hard contacts, which softens them.
free_data_check: None; the sweep (ls_iterations x ls_parallel x njmax on the shipped Franka and humanoid configs) is GPU-hours only.
method_consequence: Per-task defaults with a verified-fidelity bound; none if the behaviour change is negligible.
positioning: off-radar for LLM labs; lab-adjacent to engine builders

quote: 252x for locomotion, and 475x for manipulation tasks [MuJoCo Warp over MJX, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell]; Isaac Lab Franka cube-env settings: dt = 1/120 s, num_substeps = 2, MJWarp solver iterations = 20, line-search iterations = 100, njmax = 2000, nconmax = 1000, impratio = 1000.0; [hydroelastic contacts] ultimately achieving better sim-to-real transfer
observation: The Newton 1.0 launch reports three-digit speedups and the exact solver caps they were measured under but no accuracy, convergence or real-transfer number at those caps; the validation sentence is a partner's intention (Lightwheel to 'advance solver calibration', TRI to 'advance solver development and contact modeling'). Missed by the W41 harvest.
who_strains: NVIDIA Newton, DeepMind MuJoCo, Isaac Lab; partners (Lightwheel, TRI, Skild AI, Samsung)
question: Speedup at what fidelity? Convergence and contact error at the solver caps GPU engines advertise.
density_hint: Newton 1.0; MJWarp docs; GPUPhysBench 2609.35639; Acosta et al. RA-L 2022 (impacts wrong in Drake, MuJoCo, Bullet)
mechanism_version: Speedup is measured with iteration caps and buffer sizes that bound work per step; the unconverged residual at those caps is the fidelity price, and it is contact-dependent, so a locomotion speedup and a manipulation speedup carry different error.
free_data_check: The Isaac Lab Franka config is public; running it at 20 versus 200 iterations and comparing visited-state residuals costs GPU-hours only.
method_consequence: Engine releases report residual at advertised caps; if negligible, L5's premise weakens and the lane's first kill test fires.

quote: Running RL in the physical world is harder than in the digital world. [...] Rollouts take days rather than minutes, fewer agents run in parallel, and reward signals are noisier [Periodic Labs]; Urban driving benchmarks are saturating and the hard problems have moved [Torc]; GPU utilization up from 30 to 40 percent to approximately 90 percent [Torc]; improved RL iteration throughput by 13 percent [NVIDIA Nemotron, topology-aware placement]
observation: Industry describes RL as a production engineering problem with utilization and throughput numbers but no number for what rollouts cost per unit of policy improvement, and 'one billion simulation miles running per week' carries no fidelity statement. Missed by the W41 harvest (event 2026-08-24..26).
who_strains: Anyscale, NVIDIA, Torc Robotics, Periodic Labs, Bedrock Robotics
question: Rollout dollars per policy bit: a cost unit for RL that survives async, replay and simulation.
density_hint: W41 #2 training-time version; Thinking Machines '1 bit per episode' (W41 Q64); Arctic-SWE (one-sixth the rollouts); ReFlow
mechanism_version: Utilization is maximized by filling idle GPUs with stale or replayed rollouts, which lowers information per rollout, so utilization and learning per dollar move in opposite directions past a point that no report locates.
free_data_check: None; industry logs. Open stacks (verl, PRIME-RL, Arctic-SWE) can log rollout tokens against validation gain per step for free.
method_consequence: A reporting unit; if adopted, async schedulers are tuned on it rather than on utilization.

quote: Only 61 studies report metrics from multiple families covering sensor/perception correspondence, ADS behaviour, vehicle dynamics, or safety outcomes; this coverage does not establish causal links between discrepancies and test verdicts. [...] The findings motivate claim-specific evaluation and component-level reporting to establish which discrepancies affect testing conclusions
observation: A systematic mapping of 235 driving-simulation studies finds that no one ties a specific simulator discrepancy to a changed test verdict, the same missing link L5 names for robot RL (which artifact changed the policy), in a neighbouring field with ten times the literature.
who_strains: ADS testing community; simulation vendors (CARLA, BeamNG); by analogy robot-RL simulator users
question: Which simulator discrepancies change the verdict? Claim-specific reality-gap attribution for policies trained and tested in simulation.
density_hint: Lambertenghi, Weissl, Betz, Stocco (TUM); reality-gap survey 2510.20808 (L5 neighbours); Acosta RA-L 2022
mechanism_version: A discrepancy matters only if the policy's decisions pass through it; attribution requires re-simulating the visited states under the alternative model (L5's per-step audit), which none of the 235 studies does.
free_data_check: The mapping's study set; nothing for robot RL without the audit run.
method_consequence: A component-level reporting standard for simulation evidence; the audit becomes the attribution instrument if it separates verdict-changing discrepancies.

quote: the majority of agentic solutions contain at least one failure mode despite the complexity of agentic harness or model capacity. Moreover, we identify a positive correlation between the occurrence of data leakage failures and predictive performance, confirming the necessity to evaluate agents beyond accuracy.
observation: In agentic data science the outcome metric rewards the methodological failure (leakage raises the score), which is W41 #8's test-pass-passes-wrong-code pattern in a second domain, with a released 220-task failure analysis.
who_strains: Data-science agent benchmark owners (MLE-bench, DSBench); Kaggle-style RL environments; W41 #8
question: Does RL on predictive-score rewards teach data leakage? Methodological failure rates across base to RL checkpoints.
density_hint: Li, Xia, Gomm, Santos, Wolff, Hulsebos (CWI); W41 #8 (Humans are Missing); MLE-bench
mechanism_version: Leakage raises validation score by construction, so any score-maximizing optimizer selects for it unless the grader holds out the leak; RL on the score is such an optimizer.
free_data_check: The paper's 220-task analysis and six-failure test suite released; MLE-bench public runs; public base-to-RL pairs at inference cost.
method_consequence: Leak-detecting graders in RL environments if the RL arm rises; none otherwise.

quote: The instrument did not meet its preregistered calibration criterion: agreement with adjudicated labels was 4% to 60% against a required 80%, and inter-rater agreement was weak (kappa = 0.154). [...] a process measure judged by a language model partly reflects how a pull request is presented rather than the verification work behind it.
observation: A preregistered LLM-judged process instrument on 1,454 matched agent and human pull requests failed its own calibration and reports that presentation, not verification work, drives the judge; a direct caution for every LLM-judged process metric (overclaiming, bloat, rubric) in the W41 set.
who_strains: PR-quality instrument builders; the 'Humans are Missing' line; process-reward designers
question: Do LLM-judged process metrics measure the process or the presentation? Calibration of agent-PR instruments against a human reference.
density_hint: Dautovi, Wu; Humans are Missing 2608.12355 (W41 #8); Agentic Rubrics 2601.04171; 2610.18497 (judges follow the reference on tool-call arguments)
mechanism_version: The judge reads the diff and description; an agent PR is formatted to look verified (test file present, linked issue) and the judge's label follows the surface features the deterministic signal cannot see.
free_data_check: 1,454 matched pairs and the 25-PR adjudicated reference set; rerunning other judges on them is inference cost only.
method_consequence: Process rewards for coding agents need a mechanically decided component; W41 #8's bloat and inconsistency judges need the same calibration before they are rewards.
